title: Vitamin A Deficiency in Children
subject: Paediatrics
summary: Vitamin A deficiency impairs epithelial integrity, causing night blindness, xerophthalmia and increased infection risk. Diagnosis relies on clinical signs and limited lab tests; treatment is high‑dose vitamin A and addressing underlying causes.

sections.p: A state of inadequate retinol or provitamin A carotenoids leading to functional deficiency of vitamin A.
b: Clinical diagnosis: night blindness (nyctalopia) or xerophthalmia (Bitot's spots, corneal ulceration).
Serum retinol < 0.70 µmol/L confirms deficiency when clinical signs are absent.

sections.p: WHO classifies ocular involvement into stages 0‑V; systemic severity is judged by presence of ocular signs and growth failure.
b: Stage 0: No ocular signs.
Stage I: Night blindness only.
Stage II: Conjunctival xerosis, Bitot's spots.
Stage III: Corneal xerosis.
Stage IV: Corneal ulceration < 1/3 diameter.
Stage V: Corneal ulceration ≥ 1/3 diameter or perforation.

sections.p: Insufficient intake is the commonest cause, especially in low‑resource settings where diets lack animal‑source foods.
b: Inadequate dietary intake (e.g., cereal‑based diets, lack of dairy, eggs, liver).
Malabsorption (celiac disease, cystic fibrosis, chronic diarrhoea).
Infections increasing demand or loss (measles, HIV, TB, chronic malaria).
Low‑birth‑weight infants with depleted stores.
Use of unfortified oil or herbal remedies that interfere with absorption.

sections.p: Early ocular signs progress to systemic effects on skin, immunity and growth.
b: Night blindness – patient reports difficulty seeing at dusk.
Bitot's spots – foamy, whitish patches on temporal conjunctiva.
Dry, keratinised skin (hyperkeratosis) on palms and soles.
Recurrent respiratory infections due to squamous metaplasia of airway epithelium.
Growth retardation and anemia in severe, chronic cases.

t.b: Is there biochemical deficiency? < 0.70 µmol/L confirms VAD when ocular signs are absent.
Does the epithelium show keratinisation? Presence of squamous cells supports diagnosis.
Are there associated anemia or infection? Helps identify co‑morbidities.

sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening if untreated.
b: Corneal ulceration progressing to perforation (Stage IV‑V).
Severe respiratory infection with airway obstruction from metaplasia.
Sepsis in malnourished children with impaired immunity.

sections.p: Treat deficiency promptly, then address underlying causes and prevent recurrence.
b: Give vitamin A even if serum retinol unavailable when ocular signs present.
Treat co‑existing infections (e.g., measles, pneumonia) with appropriate antibiotics or antivirals.
Nutritional counselling: introduce vitamin‑A‑rich foods (orange‑fleshed sweet potatoes, mangoes, liver, eggs).
Avoid unnecessary parenteral vitamin A unless oral route is impossible; high‑dose intramuscular can cause toxicity.

sections.p: Monitor ocular healing and growth; integrate supplementation into routine child health programs.
b: Re‑examine eyes 2 weeks after dosing; expect resolution of night blindness and Bitot's spots.
Fortify staple foods (oil, flour) with vitamin A where feasible.
Educate caregivers on dietary sources and the importance of measles vaccination.

sections.p: Conditions that also cause conjunctival changes or night vision problems.
b: Measles‑related conjunctivitis – presents with red eyes, Koplik spots, but lacks Bitot's spots and keratinisation.
Dry eye syndrome – gritty sensation, but no foamy patches and occurs in older patients.
Vitamin B2 (riboflavin) deficiency – angular cheilitis, not night blindness.

sections.p: Laboratory and clinical findings may be deceptive in certain settings.
b: Serum retinol can be normal during acute infection (acute‑phase response) despite tissue deficiency.
Bitot's spots may be absent in early deficiency; rely on night blindness history.
Hyperkeratosis of skin can be caused by zinc deficiency; assess dietary history.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe respiratory distress from airway metaplasia.
Signs of sepsis in a malnourished child.

faq.q: Why does vitamin A deficiency cause night blindness?
faq.a: Retinal pigment (11‑cis‑retinal) is needed for phototransduction; deficiency reduces rhodopsin, impairing low‑light vision.

faq.q: Can vitamin A supplementation cause toxicity?
faq.a: Acute toxicity is rare with WHO dosing; chronic excess from fortified foods can cause liver damage, so avoid daily high‑dose regimens.

faq.q: What is the role of measles vaccination in preventing VAD complications?
faq.a: Measles depletes vitamin A stores and increases ocular damage; vaccination reduces this risk and is part of WHO VAD control strategy.

exam: A 2‑year‑old presents with night blindness and Bitot's spots – what is your immediate management and why? — Give WHO high‑dose oral vitamin A regimen; treat any infection; explain that ocular signs indicate systemic deficiency.

How would you differentiate vitamin A deficiency from measles‑related conjunctivitis in a child with red eyes? — Look for Bitot's spots, night blindness, and absence of Koplik spots; measles has fever, cough, and a maculopapular rash.

A child with severe malnutrition has a serum retinol of 0.6 µmol/L but no ocular signs – do you treat? — Yes, give prophylactic high‑dose vitamin A because biochemical deficiency predicts future ocular disease.
What are the WHO staging criteria for xerophthalmia and how does each stage guide treatment? — Stages I‑III require a single dose; stages IV‑V need repeat dosing and urgent ophthalmology referral.

Why is oral vitamin A preferred over intramuscular in most low‑resource settings? — Oral is safe, inexpensive, and avoids injection‑site complications; IM is reserved when vomiting precludes oral intake.

A child with VAD also has chronic diarrhoea – how does this affect your management? — Treat diarrhoea to improve absorption, give vitamin A after stabilising fluid/electrolytes, and consider zinc supplementation.
What public‑health measures reduce community‑wide vitamin A deficiency? — Biannual mass supplementation, food fortification, promotion of vitamin‑A‑rich diets, and measles vaccination.
